sources.title: Étienne de la Vaissière: Xiongnu
sources.note: Encyclopaedia Iranica synthesis used only for the overview and override summary: the 48 split, settlement within northern China, early-third-century loss of the last chanyu, continued identity, and caution about westward migration or simple Hun equations.

sources.title: Rafe de Crespigny: The Division and Destruction of the Xiongnu Confederacy
sources.note: ANU study, checked against the cached six-page PDF, used for Bi’s 48/49 breakaway, the 50 settlement, the initial eight divisions, and the political distinction between rulers and ordinary pastoral communities.

sources.title: Rafe de Crespigny: Northern Frontier, The Policies and Strategy of the Later Han Empire
sources.note: Open ANU monograph used for Later Han frontier bargaining, rebellions in 109 to 110, 124 and 140, abandoned commanderies, and the dependent chanyu regime.

sources.title: Rafe de Crespigny: A Steppe Too Far
sources.note: ANU frontier study used for Tanshihuai’s Xianbei power, the disastrous 177 expedition with Southern Xiongnu cavalry, and the later contraction of control.

sources.title: Rafe de Crespigny: The Three Kingdoms and Western Jin, Part I
sources.note: Open East Asian History article used for the 188 to 216 collapse, Cao Cao’s northern order, and the historical setting of the Five Divisions.

sources.title: Rafe de Crespigny: The Three Kingdoms and Western Jin, Part II
sources.note: Open East Asian History article used for Western Jin’s northern frontier, later third-century Xiongnu and Xianbei unrest, and the limits of central control.

sources.title: Hou Hanshu: Account of the Southern Xiongnu
sources.note: Chinese Text Project primary text used for the Southern chanyu’s ranks, marriage clans, oral adjudication, assemblies and annual rites. It is a Chinese court history and is read critically.

sources.title: Book of Later Han, volume 89: Treatise on the Southern Xiongnu
sources.note: Modern parallel presentation used to check the court-history passages on supervision, hostages, provisions, elite gift distributions, frontier markets, assemblies and sport.

sources.title: Dongguan Hanji: Southern Chanyu
sources.note: Chinese Text Project primary fragment used for the exact Classical Chinese writing sample and its description of Three Dragons sacrifice, horse racing and camel contests. It is not an indigenous Xiongnu-language document.

sources.title: Jin Shu, volume 101
sources.note: Later official history used cautiously for Five Divisions settlements in the Fen River region and the elite education and hostage experience attributed to Liu Yuan; its dynastic storytelling and retrospective pedigree claims are not treated as ordinary biography.

sources.title: OpenStax World History: The Steppes
sources.note: Peer-reviewed open textbook used for clan-scale pastoral life, early practical learning, hostage education, trade and the fluid frontier; its broad steppe generalizations are explicitly labelled as context.

sources.title: Early Nomads of the Eastern Steppe and Their Tentative Connections in the West
sources.note: Cambridge peer-reviewed synthesis used for the Southern buffer polity, pastoral and agricultural economy, separate Xianbei rise, and the warning that archaeological cultures rarely map neatly onto named historical groups.

sources.title: Bryan K. Miller: Xiongnu, The World’s First Nomadic Empire
sources.note: Oxford scholarly monograph used for mobile imperial organization and the long Xiongnu political background; claims are limited to inherited institutions rather than projected unchanged into every second-century household.

sources.title: Archaeological Investigations of Xiongnu-Hun Cultural Connections
sources.note: University of Minnesota dissertation used narrowly for the Budongdou Southern Xiongnu burial group, animal offerings, pottery, iron objects, paired burial and the larger problem of assigning mixed frontier remains.

sources.title: Economic Diversification Supported the Growth of Mongolia’s Nomadic Empires
sources.note: Peer-reviewed isotope study used only as earlier and northern Xiongnu background for mixed millet and animal-food consumption; it is not treated as a Southern Xiongnu menu from Ordos or Shanxi.

sources.title: Dairy Pastoralism Sustained Eastern Eurasian Steppe Populations for 5,000 Years
sources.note: Peer-reviewed biomolecular study used for the long steppe dairy tradition, explicitly separated from direct proof of one Southern Xiongnu meal.

sources.title: Clothes from the Xiongnu Wardrobe Based on Noin-Ula Finds
sources.note: Peer-reviewed textile study used as earlier elite Xiongnu comparison for caftans, trousers, felt, fur and imported silk; Noin-Ula is neither a Southern Xiongnu settlement nor an ordinary wardrobe.

sources.title: Fortified Settlements and the Settlement System in the Northern Zone of the Han Empire
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Antiquity study used for the varied hierarchy and imperial planning of Han frontier settlements, while preserving the difference between Han administrative sites and Southern Xiongnu domestic space.

sources.title: Review of Bronzes du style de l’Ordos
sources.note: Scholarly review used to warn that the broad “Ordos” label mixes several styles and sometimes different named groups, limiting confident ethnic assignment of material culture.

sources.title: Dental Caries Prevalence in Xiongnu Population from Mongolia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed paleopathology study used for dental disease and carbohydrate evidence in Xiongnu-period Mongolian remains spanning the second century BCE to second century CE; it does not document Southern Xiongnu medicine.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art: Model of a Latrine and Pigsty
sources.note: Museum catalogue used for the existence of a first-century Eastern Han funerary latrine-and-pigsty model, explicitly not evidence for a Southern Xiongnu household toilet.

sources.title: Excreted and Left Untreated? Human and Animal Waste from Dunhuang to Laozi
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study used for rare Eastern Han sanitation evidence: a Yinan privy image, a Dunhuang relay-station latrine and hygiene sticks, plus the limits of reconstructing general practice.

proposedOverrides.summary: A Han-aligned frontier polity became supervised Five Divisions after the chanyu office ended in 216; communities continued under Wei and Jin.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id southern-xiongnu is indexed circa 100 to 300 CE and occurs only in the 100 and 200 snapshots among the audited seams.

Both exact features are the same one-part, one-ring, 20-position Polygon, bounds [98.29358293582936, 39.41380788564797, 106.35766357663579, 42.82299046120785], with coordinate hash eb99737ebad52a00066b46c0925c947a0a38598b34652faa036b2a83bb48bfca.

Ejin/Khara-Khoto, Badain Jaran and northern Alxa test inside; Ordos, Hohhot, Shuofang, Datong, Taiyuan, Pingyang, Ye and Luoyang test outside. The imported geometry is therefore seriously displaced west of documented Southern Xiongnu settlements.

The political formation began with Bi’s breakaway in 48/49 and Han agreement in 50. The chanyu office effectively ended in 216; the atlas continues the id to 300, covering communities reorganized under Cao Wei and Western Jin.
Earlier xiongnu and xiongnu-bc200 records, the independent Xianbei, Cao Wei, Jin and later Han-Zhao remain distinct. No appliesTo alias is added.
All bounds, hashes and point tests describe imported display geometry only; none establishes sovereignty, ethnicity, language, migration or modern territorial claims.
